title: food as practice
hook: a phone propped against a glass, a fork moving on its own: Charaka's rules for eating describe the opposite

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice meant measure: matra, the amount your own fire digests well, with room left over. Did you stop halfway and ask if you were still hungry? Day one thousand three hundred nine.

A phone propped against a water glass. A video playing. A fork going up and down more or less on its own, and at some point the plate is empty and it's hard to say what was on it. That's an ordinary lunch now, and nobody needs a lecture about it. But it's interesting to set beside a passage in the Charaka Samhita that lays out how to eat. Not what. How. Read today, it sounds startlingly current. It closes a week that walked through the seasons and into food. Today, the way of eating.
screen: `A PHONE AGAINST A WATER GLASS.` → `NOT WHAT TO EAT. HOW.` → `TODAY, THE WAY OF EATING.`

segments.voice: In its section on how food should be taken, Charaka gives a set of guidelines. Paraphrased, they run like this. Eat food that is warm. Eat in measure, yesterday's word. Eat after the last meal has been digested, not on top of it. Eat in a pleasant place, with what you need at hand. Eat neither too fast nor too slowly. Don't talk or laugh through the meal. Eat with your mind on the food, knowing what suits you. What stands out? First, almost none of this is about ingredients. It's about attention, pace and place. The same plate of food, eaten in a rush while scrolling, or eaten slowly at a table, is in this view not quite the same meal. Second, the rules aren't harsh. A pleasant place is one of them. The text wants you comfortable. Third, the week behind us has been building to this. Spring's lighter food, summer's water, the low fire of the rains, autumn's cooling: each season changed what to eat. Bhrigu showed that food is worth reverence. Measure said how much. And today Charaka says how. Here the Ayurvedic lens meets household practice. In some Hindu homes, before the first bite, someone says a verse from the Bhagavad Gita, chapter four: the offering is Brahman, the food offered is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. Whether or not words are said, the pause itself does what Charaka asks. It puts the mind on the food before the hand moves.
screen: `WARM, AND AFTER THE LAST MEAL` · `A PLEASANT PLACE, AN EASY PACE` · `THE MIND ON THE FOOD` · `A VERSE BEFORE THE FIRST BITE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one sip, eaten like a meal. If there's water or tea near you, pick it up. Look at it first. Feel its weight and its warmth or cool in your hand. Take one sip, and keep it in your mouth a moment before you swallow. Follow it down. Then set the cup down, and sit with whatever's left: the taste, the warmth, the quiet. If nothing's at hand, do the same with a breath. If you pray, you can say a line of grace your family uses. The bell holds the time.
Food as practice. Charaka's way of eating: warm food, after the last meal is digested, in a pleasant place, at an easy pace, with the mind on the food. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. Today, eat one meal, or just its first few bites, with the screen face down and your mind on the food. Day one thousand three hundred nine.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda eat warm food at an easy pace, after the previous meal has digested, in a pleasant place and with attention, as Charaka describes; in some Hindu homes a verse from the Gita (4.24) is said before eating.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Vimanasthana 1 (the method of eating: warm, unctuous, in measure, after the previous meal is digested, non-antagonistic, in a pleasant place with all accessories, not too fast or slow, without talking or laughing, with concentration, knowing what suits oneself)

notes: Week-end day (1303–1309): the teach looks back over spring, summer, rains, autumn, Bhrigu (1307) and measure (1308).
Charaka Vimanasthana 1 (around 1.24–25): confirm the list as paraphrased. 'Unctuous' and 'not contrary in potency' were left out of the spoken list for simplicity; confirm the omission is acceptable.

Gita 4.24 said before meals: confirm 'in some Hindu homes'. Paraphrase of the verse should be checked against the Sanskrit. The verse has been used on earlier days (e.g. 173, 966–967, 1200); here it appears only as the meal-time verse.
